    * feat(core): preload deferred tools within a context-window threshold
    
    Adds tools.toolSearch.threshold (default 10, percent of the context
    window). At session start, when the combined estimated schema footprint
    of every deferred tool - bundled built-ins and MCP alike - fits within
    the budget, all are revealed upfront so the declaration list stays
    stable for the whole session and prefix KV caches survive; otherwise
    everything stays deferred. Set 0 to always defer. Mirrors Claude Code's
    ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto threshold mode, extended to bundled deferred
    tools because here every reveal rewrites the declaration list and busts
    the prompt-cache prefix.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    
    * feat(core): log deferred-tool preload budget decision
    
    Emit debugLogger diagnostics in preloadDeferredToolsWithinBudget covering
    the computed budget, estimated token footprint, candidate count, and which
    branch of the all-or-nothing gate was taken (no candidates, over budget, or
    preloaded). Lets an operator diagnosing session-startup cost tell from debug
    logs whether the deferred set fit the budget or was left behind ToolSearch,
    without adding temporary instrumentation. No behavior change.

    The threshold setting is a percentage of the context window but had no
    upper bound, so a value like 200 (a typo or misreading of the "(%)"
    label) made the preload budget exceed the whole window and
    unconditionally preloaded every deferred tool — the opposite of the
    prefix-stability the threshold buys.

      like autoCompactThreshold) and regenerate the VS Code settings schema.
    - Add a symmetric runtime upper guard next to the existing
      'thresholdPercent <= 0' lower guard in client.ts, clamping to 100% so a
      hand-edited settings file cannot slip a larger budget past validation.
    
    Adds a client test asserting a 200% threshold clamps to a full-context
    budget.
    
    * test(core): cover configured preload budget
    
    * fix(tool-search): harden preload threshold
    
    * test(tool-search): cover preload exclusions

evidence_units.claim: The checked-in design identifies the resource tradeoff: deferred-tool reveals rewrite the function-declaration prefix and invalidate prompt KV cache; it specifies a 10% context-window threshold, a union budget over bundled and MCP tools, all-or-nothing reveal, a zero opt-out, and session-start-only application.
Core ConfigParameters accepts a toolSearchThreshold percentage, Config stores it with a default of 10, and getToolSearchThreshold exposes the effective value to runtime consumers.
The CLI config assembly passes settings.tools.toolSearch.threshold into ConfigParameters and supplies 0 instead when bareMode or safeMode is active.
The settings schema defines the deferred-tool threshold as a number with default 10 and a JSON-schema minimum of 0 and maximum of 100; the generated VS Code schema mirrors type, bounds, and default.

The session-start budget adapter skips when ToolSearch is absent, the threshold is non-finite or non-positive, or the context window is invalid; otherwise it clamps the percentage to 100, selects configured contextWindowSize or tokenLimit(model,'input'), and passes floor(contextWindow*boundedPercent/100) to the registry.
The model input-token-limit helper returns a known model limit when available and otherwise falls back to DEFAULT_TOKEN_LIMIT, which is the fallback used by the client budget adapter.

startChat invokes the new deferred_tool_preload stage after tool_registry_warm and resume_deferred_tool_reveal but before deferred_reminder_setup; setTools subsequently obtains the declaration list from the resulting registry state.

Therefore revealing a candidate makes its schema part of subsequent declarations, while always-loaded and visible tools do not need preload budget.

When ToolSearch is available, deferred-reminder setup filters out already-revealed tools; when ToolSearch is unavailable, the existing branch eagerly reveals all deferred summaries and returns no reminder. title: [Linux Desktop] local stdio MCP launch inherits unrelated app-server file descriptors into MCP servers and their children
before: The local Unix stdio launcher constructed a child command with piped stdin/stdout/stderr and a new process group, but did not set a descriptor-inheritance policy. The shared command builder therefore retained its default DescriptorPolicy::Inherit, allowing inheritable, unrelated descriptors held by the orchestrator to reach the local MCP server and any descendants it launched. The local runtime path selected LocalStdioServerLauncher for local stdio MCP configurations and passed that command through RmcpClient to the launcher.
after: The local Unix stdio launcher sets DescriptorPolicy::StdioOnly on every locally constructed MCP command. The existing Unix spawn backend then closes inheritable descriptors other than the explicit transport stdio before exec, while retaining the internal exec-error reporting path; the macOS native backend uses its close-on-exec-default path. The server and descendants therefore inherit only the explicitly wired stdio transport, while the existing process group, arguments, environment, working directory, MCP protocol exchange, and launch-error behavior remain intact. The change is guarded by cfg(unix); Windows behavior is intentionally unchanged and remains a deferred handle-allowlist concern.
diff: Commit afe4249cfe, parent b4b30dd5eb9994ddc51f915ecd74e9a8c1d93248, modifies codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/stdio_server_launcher.rs by adding Unix DescriptorPolicy support and applying command.descriptor_policy(DescriptorPolicy::StdioOnly) inside the local command builder. It adds codex-rs/rmcp-client/tests/stdio_descriptor_boundary.rs, a Unix-only integration test that creates inheritable pipe, socket, and file descriptors, verifies an unfiltered control launch sees them, then exercises absolute, relative, and shell-fallback local launches and asserts that neither the MCP server nor its descendant sees them. The test also checks MCP communication, arguments, environment, working directory, stderr, parent descriptor ownership after shutdown, and direct exec-failure reporting. The same integration test runs local MCP launches through absolute, relative, and shell-fallback command forms, initializes the MCP connection, lists tools, calls the probe tool, and asserts that both the server and its descendant observe [false, false, false] for the pipe/socket/file sentinels while stdio round-trip, stderr, cwd, environment, argument handling, and request arguments remain correct.

After shutting down the MCP clients, the test reads the parent descriptors' F_GETFD flags and asserts they remain open and unchanged, proving descriptor cleanup is confined to the spawned process rather than mutating parent ownership.

A second Unix integration test creates an executable script whose interpreter is missing, then asserts that local stdio client creation returns an error; its comment specifically protects direct exec-failure reporting when descriptor cleanup is enabled.
